slides.title: QHAG: Quarterly Highly Achievable Goal
slides.headline: QHAG: Quarterly Highly Achievable Goal
notes: The QHAG turns the 1HAG into this quarter’s targets and priorities.
Individual quarterly priorities come from the QHAG next.
body: Set this quarter’s targets, month by month, and the priorities that deliver the annual plan.

artwork.alt: The cascade from BHAG to priorities: BHAG, 3HAG, 1HAG, QHAG, then individual quarterly priorities. Each level is built from the one above it and directs the one below. QHAG is highlighted: this is where we are.

slides.title: Your QHAG on one page.
slides.headline: Your QHAG on one page.

artwork.alt: Example QHAG page for the same subscription business, Q1 January to March 2027. 1, Numbers for the quarter and each month, each with an owner. Gross revenue $1.2 million, Andrew. Profit margin 5%, Allison. Cash $1.0 million, Allison. Widgets: 2,100 subscription leads and 840 marketing qualified subscription leads, Chris. 210 new subscriptions, Andrew. 195 activated subscriptions, Jen. 4,800 collected payments, Allison. Profit per subscription $38 for the quarter ($10, $13 and $15 by month), Allison. Head count 32, Pat. 2, Priorities, each supporting an annual priority. #1 remove the first 2 days of activation, Jen, done by February 28. Success: days to activate 5 or fewer achieved by March 31. #2 hire the first account executive, Andrew, done by March 15. Success: new MRR at or above $25K a month achieved by June 30. #3 move the 100 largest customers to automatic billing, Allison, done by March 31. Success: days to collect 20 or fewer achieved by June 30.

hotspots.tip: Jim Collins’s economic engine, from Good to Great. It is the one profit ratio that, raised steadily over time, does the most to drive your economics. Here, profit per subscription: profit divided by the average number of active subscriptions. Allison owns hitting the target.

notes: Same page again, for the next quarter, month by month. Every number has an owner.
Don’t just divide the year by four. Ask how the quarter really builds, month by month.
Each quarterly priority moves an annual priority forward.

slides.title: What are your quarterly targets?
slides.headline: What are your quarterly targets?
notes: Ask for the quarter’s numbers. Each leader can post theirs in private mode first.
Ask questions about the math rather than telling them it is wrong. Ask who owns each number.
Compare answers and assumptions. Agree on the period, gross revenue, ending cash, widgets and head count, month by month.
Use the same widget definitions as the 3-year plan. Distinguish new activity from cumulative totals.
Ask who owns each metric. Wait for each owner to claim responsibility aloud. Record the owner beside the target.
Reconcile the targets with the longer-term plan. Discuss seasonality and assumptions rather than dividing targets mechanically.
Revenue is a period flow. Cash is an ending balance. Do not divide every target by four or add up successive cash balances.
Reconcile with the 1HAG: is each quarter’s target big enough to stay on track for the year? If the later quarters must carry more than their share of the year, ask what makes them steeper.
Profit per subscription ramps through the year: $10 to $15 a month this quarter, $25 a month by December. That is the annualized December rate: $300 a year.
When the team has no data for a number, set a best estimate and track it. The next status review asks where the estimate was wrong.

artwork.alt: The QHAG page’s block 1, Numbers. It shows gross revenue, profit margin, cash, the widgets, profit per subscription and head count. Each has a number for the quarter and each month, and an owner.

hotspots.tip: Jim Collins’s economic engine, from Good to Great. It is the one profit ratio that, raised steadily over time, does the most to drive your economics. Here, profit per subscription: profit divided by the average number of active subscriptions. Allison owns hitting the target.

slides.support: Confirm the quarter and its end date.
body: Gross revenue, margin, ending cash, each widget and head count, month by month.
Name an owner for every number.
No data yet? Set your best estimate, then track it.
Is each target big enough to keep you on track for your 1HAG?

slides.title: What is the #1 priority for the quarter?
slides.headline: What is the #1 priority for the quarter?
notes: Every leader independently lists what the company must accomplish this quarter to deliver a 1HAG priority, then shares.
At a quarterly, add the worries and opportunities circled on the Market Map to the candidates.

Run the six questions from the “Pick the priorities that contribute most to success” slide on each candidate. Hover over “six questions” to show them. In a 90-day window, “How soon will we see it?” counts for more.
The team ranks the survivors together. At least 80 percent agreement supports 100 percent commitment.
Challenge vague aspirations and repeated revenue targets. Ask which specific work will produce the result.
Invite debate and explore disagreement. Do not let the CEO answer for everyone. Ask holdouts what the team may have missed. Seek full commitment after discussion.
Ask an owner to claim the #1 priority aloud. Check they have the capacity and skills. Name one accountable leader. If only the CEO can own it, name the leadership gap first.
Agree on the done-by date, the measure of success and the achieved-by date.
slides.support: What must be accomplished now to deliver the annual plan?
body: List candidates from your 1HAG priorities. Test each with the six questions, then rank.
Agree on the owner, done-by date, measure of success and achieved-by date.

artwork.alt: The QHAG page’s block 2, Priorities, with priority #1 highlighted. Remove the first 2 days of activation, owner Jen, done by February 28. Success: days to activate 5 or fewer by March 31.

tip: What does it build or move?
How much will it move a critical number?
How soon will we see it?
Who can own it and succeed?

slides.title: What else must be accomplished this quarter?
slides.headline: What else must be accomplished this quarter?
notes: At a quarterly, list last quarter’s open priorities first. They stay on the new QHAG until their number has moved.
Take the next candidates in rank order from the same list.
Discuss disagreement, tradeoffs, dependencies and capacity. Agree on the rank together.
An owner claims the priority aloud. Agree on the done-by date, the measure and the achieved-by date.
The achieved-by date can fall after the quarter ends. The work is done this quarter. The priority stays open on the next QHAG until the number has moved.
Repeat for priorities 2 to 5 in order. Five is a ceiling. Stop when the list covers the critical work.
slides.support: Ideally 3, up to 5 company priorities in total, including #1.
body: Connect each to an annual priority. Give each an owner, a done-by date, a measure of success and an achieved-by date.

artwork.alt: The QHAG page’s block 2, Priorities, all three shown. #1 is above. The next is hire the first account executive, Andrew, done by March 15. Success: new MRR of $25K a month or more by June 30. The last is move the 100 largest customers to automatic billing, Allison, done by March 31. Success: days to collect 20 or fewer by June 30.

slides.title: Does your QHAG pass?
slides.headline: Does your QHAG pass?
notes: Read the QHAG aloud, top to bottom, then run the seven checks.

Revenue and the widgets you count add up: the 3 months equal the quarter. Cash and head count are balances: the quarter ends at month 3’s number. Margin is for the whole quarter: the quarter’s profit over the quarter’s revenue.
Anything that fails goes on the homework list with an owner.
slides.support: Read it aloud before you move on.
body: Every number and priority has one owner with capacity.
Each priority advances a 1HAG priority, with success measured by a critical number, preferably.
Each priority is done by quarter end, with a target and an achieved-by date.
Each priority moves its number enough, and soon enough to see.
The targets are big enough to stay on track for the 1HAG.
The months build to the quarter. Revenue and widgets you count add up. Cash and head count match month 3.

artwork.alt: The planning cascade with the 3HAG, 1HAG and QHAG checked. Individual priorities are still to come.
